Puerility means childishness — specifically, the quality of thinking, speaking, or behaving in a way that is silly, trivial, or immature, especially when the person doing it is old enough to know better.

The key thing to understand right away is that puerility is not simply about being young. A child being childish is just... normal. Puerility carries a sting of criticism — it is what you call it when an adult, or someone in a serious situation, acts with the silliness or immaturity of a small child. That gap between what is expected and what is actually happening is the heart of the word.

Think of it this way: if a five-year-old sticks out their tongue at someone, that's just childhood. If a forty-year-old does it in a board meeting, that is puerility.

Puerility can show up in several overlapping ways. It helps to see each one clearly:

1. Silly or trivial behavior that belongs in a playground, not in adult life.
A manager who sulks and gives his team the silent treatment because a meeting didn't go his way is displaying puerility. The behavior is petty, small, and beneath the maturity expected of his role.

2. Humor or jokes that are crude, low, or infantile — especially in a setting that demands seriousness.
If someone responds to a thoughtful, serious conversation with toilet humor or ridiculous giggling, the puerility of their response stands out sharply against the gravity of the moment.

3. Arguments or opinions that are shallow and underdeveloped — like something a child might say.
Imagine a public debate on a complex issue where one speaker simply calls the other names and repeats the same weak point over and over. A commentator might say, "The puerility of his argument was embarrassing." Here, puerility means the argument had no depth, no sophistication — it was the intellectual equivalent of a child's reasoning.

4. Written or artistic work that feels thin, silly, or lacking in any serious thought.
A critic might describe a novel that relies entirely on cheap gags, obvious jokes, and no real substance as a work of puerility — meaning it feels like something produced by or for a very young mind, not a mature one.
The Tone and Weight of the Word

Puerility is never a neutral word. It is always a criticism, and a fairly sharp one. When you use it (or when you hear it used), it signals:

  • Disapproval. The speaker finds the behavior unworthy and beneath the standard expected.
  • A sense of contrast. There is always an implied gap — this person should know better, this moment deserved better, this work could have been better.
  • Mild contempt. Not always, but often. Calling something puerility is a way of dismissing it — of saying it doesn't deserve to be taken seriously because it is so childishly trivial.

It is a formal, literary word. You won't hear it in casual conversation very often. You are more likely to encounter it in newspaper opinion columns, literary criticism, political commentary, or formal essays — places where writers want to express sharp disapproval in an elevated, precise way.
Singular vs. Plural — A Small but Important Note

In its singular form, puerility refers to the overall quality or state of being childish.
"The puerility of his response shocked everyone in the room."
(Here, puerility is the general quality — the atmosphere of childishness.)

In its plural form, puerilities, the word refers to specific individual instances of childish behavior or remarks — like counting the separate silly things someone did or said.
"His speech was full of puerilities — petty jabs, silly voices, and pointless digressions."
(Here, puerilities are the concrete, countable acts of childishness.)
How It Differs from Similar Words

These words are close neighbors, but they are not identical:

Childishness is the everyday, plain English version of puerility. They mean essentially the same thing, but puerility is more formal, more literary, and carries a slightly sharper edge of intellectual criticism.

Immaturity is broader. It can describe emotional underdevelopment, social awkwardness, or a general lack of life experience. Puerility is more specific — it zeroes in on silliness, triviality, and the specific playfulness of a child in a context where it doesn't belong.

Silliness is lighter. You can be silly and it can be charming or affectionate. Puerility is heavier — it always implies that the silliness is unwelcome, out of place, or beneath the person showing it.

Juvenility is a close cousin but slightly softer. Juvenility can sometimes be used in a neutral or even fond sense (the juvenility of youth). Puerility is almost always used critically.
A Few Examples to Lock It In

• "The committee expected a serious proposal. What they received was an embarrassing display of puerility — doodles on the slides, a poorly rehearsed skit, and no real data."
  • "She was tired of his puerility — every time she brought up a genuine problem in the relationship, he would change the subject or make a joke."
  • "The film critic dismissed the movie not for being too dark or too violent, but for its sheer puerility — everything in it was shallow, noisy, and mindless."
  • "The puerilities of the debate — the name-calling, the mockery, the obvious dodging of real questions — left voters deeply disheartened."

If you ever need to recall this word in an instant, remember this:

Puerility is childishness where childishness has no business being.

It is the silliness, triviality, and immaturity of a child — worn, embarrassingly, by someone or something that should have long since grown out of it.
